subject: Copywriting
title: Claude Hopkins: Scientific Advertising
description: A 60-second lesson on Claude Hopkins: Scientific Advertising.

hook.text: In 1923, Claude Hopkins wrote a 70-page book that changed advertising forever. He demanded proof, not creativity.

buildup.text: Hopkins invented the coupon—a trackable device to measure which ads actually sold. He turned advertising into science.

discovery.text: He tested headlines, offers, and images with split runs. The winning version ran; the loser died.

twist.text: Hopkins also invented the free sample campaign. He gave away Pepsodent toothpaste and hooked millions on brushing.

climax.text: David Ogilvy said nobody should be allowed in advertising until they'd read Scientific Advertising seven times.

punchline.text: Test everything. Hopkins proved that advertising is math.

quiz.question: What did Claude Hopkins invent to track ad performance?

details.summary: Claude Hopkins wrote 'Scientific Advertising' in 1923, arguing that advertising should be tested, measured, and optimized like a science. He pioneered coupon tracking, test markets, and headline testing — techniques that became the foundation of modern data-driven marketing.
details.whyItMatters: Hopkins transformed advertising from art into measurable science. Every A/B test, conversion tracking pixel, and performance campaign traces its lineage back to his principles.
takeaways: His 1923 book remains a foundational text for direct-response marketers
He invented coupon-based tracking to measure ad effectiveness
Hopkins insisted that every ad dollar should produce measurable results

faq.question: What is the core idea of 'Scientific Advertising'?
faq.answer: Hopkins argued that advertising is salesmanship in print and should be judged by the same standard: does it produce sales? He rejected awards and creativity for creativity's sake, insisting every element should be tested against results.

faq.question: Is 'Scientific Advertising' still relevant today?
faq.answer: Remarkably yes. The book's principles — test everything, respect the customer, focus on benefits — map directly onto modern digital marketing. David Ogilvy called it the most important book on advertising ever written.
